title: Planetary Nebula MyCn18: An Hourglass Pattern Around a Dying Star
caption: The Hourglass Nebula (MyCn18), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Hourglass Nebula, MyCn18 · constellation Musca · about 8,000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: Raghvendra Sahai and John Trauger (JPL), the WFPC2 science team, and NASA

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: An hourglass of glowing gas, its walls covered in an intricate pattern of arc-like etchings, surrounds a dying star in MyCn18. This young planetary nebula lies about 8,000 light-years away in the constellation Musca. Earlier pictures from the ground showed only a pair of large outer rings around a smaller central one, with none of the fine detail.

One theory says an hourglass forms when a fast stellar wind expands inside a slower cloud that is denser at its equator than at its poles. MyCn18 did not fit that picture neatly. The bright elliptical ring at the centre turned out to be a potato-shaped structure tilted at a very different angle from the hourglass, and the hot star thought to have ejected and lit the nebula sits clearly off centre.
Hubble also found a pair of intersecting rings near the middle that look like the rims of a smaller hourglass. An unseen companion star, and its gravity, may be needed to explain the whole structure.

understand.summary: Assembled from three images taken with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2. Light from ionised nitrogen is shown in red, hydrogen in green and doubly ionised oxygen in blue.
understand.eye: Each colour isolates the glow of a single gas, and Hubble's sharpness reveals fine etchings that are usually blurred beyond recognition in pictures taken from the ground.

behind.people: See full credit: Raghvendra Sahai and John Trauger (JPL), the WFPC2 science team, and NASA
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The etchings on the walls could be leftovers of separate shells the star threw off when it was younger, the result of unstable flows, or the work of a narrow beam of matter hitting the walls. Old Sun-like stars swell into red giants, and once one has shed its outer layers, ultraviolet light from the exposed hot core makes that material glow as a planetary nebula.
sources: NASA release: Hubble Finds an Hourglass Nebula around a Dying Star
